```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(deconflate)
```

## The problem

Single-disease impact estimates compare animals with and without a disease.
Animals with one disease are more (or less) likely to have associated
diseases, so each estimate partly reflects the impacts of those other
diseases. Adding such estimates double counts. `deconflate` adjusts
("de-conflates") the estimates so that they can be aggregated.

The package assumes no species, outcome or unit. The examples use dairy
cattle and milk yield, but any population of animals (or people) and any
additive outcome works the same way.

## A population and an impact table

The population holds what every outcome shares: the disease probabilities
and the association rows. This is the three-disease example from the
Supplementary File of Rasmussen et al. (2022):

```{r}
pop <- cm_population(
  cm_diseases(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(0.10, 0.15, 0.20), measure = "prevalence"),
  cm_associations(c("d1", "d1", "d2"), c("d2", "d3", "d3"), c(2, 1, 3), measure = "OR")
)
pop
```

Each association row relates a `disease` to the diseases it is
`associated_with`. Rows are odds ratios by default (risk ratios, risk
differences, phi coefficients, prevalences and ratios of odds ratios are
also accepted; see `?cm_associations`). A row can also be about a
combination of diseases, hold within a subgroup (`among`), be adjusted for
other diseases (`adjusted_for`), and a pair can have several rows (from
several studies), which are pooled; see `vignette("interactions")`. An odds
ratio of 1, as for d1 and d3, states that two diseases are unrelated. A pair
with no row at all is *unknown*: `deconflate()` then fills it in from the
other rows (below).

A model adds one impact table: at least one raw estimate per disease, all
in the same units. The units can be anything additive (percent of yield, kg of
milk, days, euros, a welfare score); the engine does not convert them, and
the results come back in the units supplied.

```{r}
yield <- cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(2.5, 5, 7.5),
                    outcome = "milk yield loss", units = "% of yield")
m <- cm_model(pop, yield)
m
```

The same impacts in kg give the same adjustment, in kg:

```{r}
kg <- cm_model(pop, cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(250, 500, 750),
                               units = "kg/animal/year"))
deconflate(kg)$adjusted
```

Each `deconflate()` call adjusts one impact table. For another outcome, make
another model on the same population and call `deconflate()` again:

```{r}
ci <- cm_model(pop, cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(4, 10, 2),
                               outcome = "calving interval increase", units = "days"))
deconflate(ci)$adjusted
```

The tables can also be read from CSV files (with any names) or data frames
with `cm_read_inputs()`, which checks them and reports every problem at
once (see `vignette("own-data")`):

```{r}
ex <- system.file("extdata", "five_diseases", package = "deconflate")
five <- cm_read_inputs(diseases = file.path(ex, "diseases.csv"),
                       associations = file.path(ex, "associations.csv"),
                       impacts = file.path(ex, "impacts_yield.csv"),
                       outcome = "milk yield loss", units = "% of yield")
five
```

## Adjusting impacts

```{r}
res <- deconflate(m)
res
```

`deconflate()` has one model. It describes the population by the
maximum-entropy distribution of disease combinations that matches every
association row (the distribution that assumes nothing beyond the rows),
and finds the adjusted impacts (and any interactions) that reproduce every
impact row. Up to 20 diseases it enumerates all combinations; beyond that
it uses the sampled backend of `fit_joint()`
(`vignette("thresholds-and-scaling")`).

When every association row is a crude row about a pair, every pair has one,
and every impact row is a crude or adjusted row about one disease, the
pairwise 2x2 tables give the same answer as the full distribution, and
`deconflate()` uses them directly (it still fits the distribution once, to
check that the rows can hold together). `$diagnostics$method` says which
was used:

```{r}
res$diagnostics$method
```

Leaving out the d1:d3 odds ratio makes that pair unknown:

```{r}
pop_unknown <- cm_population(pop$diseases,
                             cm_associations(c("d1", "d2"), c("d2", "d3"), c(2, 3)))
res_unknown <- deconflate(cm_model(pop_unknown, yield))
res_unknown$diagnostics$method
res_unknown$unknown_pairs
rbind(odds_ratio_1 = setNames(res$adjusted$adjusted, res$adjusted$disease),
      unknown = res_unknown$adjusted$adjusted)
```

The fit gives d1 and d3 a positive association (an odds ratio of
about 1.14), implied by their associations with d2, so the adjusted impacts
differ from those with an odds ratio of 1. Unknown is not the same as independent; see
`vignette("interactions")`.

The diagnostics report how well the adjusted impacts reconstruct the raw
ones, the condition number of the conflation matrix, and adjusted impacts
whose sign differs from the raw impact. A sign change means that the raw
impact is smaller than the associated diseases alone would produce, so the
inputs are inconsistent under the additive model (or the rows do not mean
what they were taken to mean, e.g. an adjusted estimate entered as crude):

```{r}
low_d2 <- cm_model(pop, cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(2.5, 0.2, 7.5)))
tryCatch(deconflate(low_d2), deconflate_sign_change = function(w) conditionMessage(w))
```

## Contributions

The expected aggregate impact per animal is `sum_i p_i b_i` (plus any
interaction terms). Each disease's contribution is its own term plus half of
each interaction term it is involved in, which is its Shapley value in
closed form. Contributions add up to the aggregate:

```{r}
res$contributions
res$totals
```

`raw_total` is the raw aggregate: the same model with the diseases
unrelated, which here (one crude row per disease) is `sum(p * raw)`. The
difference from `adjusted_total` is the double counting removed. In
`$contributions`, `main` is each disease's own term, `interaction` its
share of the interactions, and `raw_contribution` its contribution with the
diseases unrelated (these add up to `raw_total`). The shares are `NA` when the aggregate is zero,
since a share of zero is not defined.

`print(res)` gives the short overview above. `summary(res)` gives the full
report in sections (impacts, contributions with their parts, totals,
diagnostics and notes), and `contribution_table(res)` one table per disease
at full precision, with the same columns for every result, to write out
with `write.csv()`:

```{r}
summary(res)
contribution_table(res)
```

### Groups of diseases

Forms of one disease, such as subclinical and clinical ketosis, have their
own prevalences, associations and impacts in the literature, so they are
entered as separate diseases. `groups` reports them together: a group's
contribution is the sum of its diseases' contributions (an interaction
between them is counted wholly in the group), and with draws its interval
comes from the sum in each draw. In the global dairy inputs of Rasmussen et
al. (2024) (`warn = FALSE` hides the warning about the adjusted impacts of
a few diseases changing sign with these inputs; see "When adjusted impacts
change sign" in `vignette("own-data")`):

```{r}
gd <- deconflate(example_global_dairy("yield"), n_draws = 0, warn = FALSE,
                 groups = list(ketosis = c("SCK", "CK"), mastitis = c("SCM", "CM")))
gd$groups[, c("group", "diseases", "raw_contribution", "contribution", "share")]
```

The rows add up to the total: the groups, then each disease not in a group.
`plot(gd, type = "groups")` draws them, and `contribution_table()` names
each disease's group. How the forms overlap (clinical cases that also count
as subclinical, or each animal counted in its worst form only) is set by
the association row between them.

How robust is a ranking or a sign to one uncertain input? `cm_threshold()`
finds the input values at which the conclusion changes, for example the odds
ratio of d2 and d3 at which d1 would contribute more than d2:

```{r}
cm_threshold(m, "pair:d2:d3", c(0.1, 100), conclusion = "rank")$thresholds[
  , c("item", "status", "threshold", "description")]
```

See `vignette("thresholds-and-scaling")`.

## What an impact row means

An impact row is read as a crude or an adjusted estimate, depending on
`adjusted_for`:

* empty (the default): **crude**, the difference in the outcome between
  animals with and without the disease, not adjusted for other diseases;
* disease ids separated by `";"`, or `"all"` for every other disease:
  **adjusted**, the coefficient of the disease in an additive (linear)
  regression of the outcome on the disease and those diseases.

Ids in `adjusted_for` that are not diseases of the model (herd, parity,
...) are noted and otherwise ignored. For an adjusted estimate, the package
uses the population regression implied by the distribution of disease
combinations. This requires that the probabilities and associations
describe the source population of the estimates. Other adjusted estimates
(matched or propensity-score estimates, for example) are not supported.

A row can also be about a combination of diseases (`"d1;d2"`: animals with
both compared with animals with neither), which identifies an interaction,
and it can hold within a subgroup (`among`, e.g. `"d2"`, `"no d2"` or
`"no others"` for animals with none of the other diseases). A disease can
have several rows; when they have distributions, they are combined by
weighted least squares and `$heterogeneity` says how well they agree. See
`?cm_impacts` and `vignette("interactions")`.

A worked example: in the population above, the true additive impacts are
0.02, 0.04 and 0.06. A study of d1 that adjusted for d2, and crude studies of
d2 and d3, would report:

```{r}
truth <- c(d1 = 0.02, d2 = 0.04, d3 = 0.06)
raw <- simulate_raw_impacts(pop, truth, adjusted_for = c("d2", NA, NA))
round(raw$value, 4)
```

With `adjusted_for` recorded, the adjustment recovers the truth:

```{r}
imp_adj <- cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), raw$value, adjusted_for = c("d2", NA, NA))
m_adj <- cm_model(pop, imp_adj)
deconflate(m_adj)$adjusted
```

Treating the d1 estimate as crude adjusts it a second time for d2 and gives
the wrong answer:

```{r}
m_wrong <- cm_model(pop, cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), imp_adj$value))
deconflate(m_wrong)$adjusted$adjusted
```

## Uncertainty

When inputs have distributions (the `dist` columns of the input tables, or
`distributions` in `cm_model()`), `deconflate()` also draws them
(`n_draws = 1000` by default) and adds 95% intervals. The central estimate
always uses the point values. Without distributions no draws are run, and a
note says so (as in the results above). The five-disease example has
distributions for most inputs; 200 draws keep this example fast:

```{r}
res_five <- deconflate(five, n_draws = 200, seed = 1)
res_five
```

Pass `n_draws = 0` for point estimates only. See `vignette("uncertainty")`
for the draws, their stability checks and the sensitivity tools.

## Plots

`plot()` draws a result in base graphics; `type` chooses the plot:
`"impacts"` (the default: raw and adjusted, with the intervals from the
draws), `"contributions"` (with the raw contributions, the diseases
unrelated), `"ranks"` (how often each disease ranks 1st, 2nd, ... over the
draws) and `"rows"` (each impact row as entered and as the model fits it).
Titles and axes use the `outcome` and `units` given when the impacts are
read (`cm_read_inputs()`) or built (`cm_impacts()`); both are optional.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2}
plot(res_five)
plot(res_five, type = "contributions")
plot(res_five, type = "ranks")
```

`plot_data()` returns the data frame a plot draws (one row per point or
bar), so that the same plot can be drawn with other tools, such as ggplot2:

```{r}
head(plot_data(res_five, "ranks"))
```

## Event impacts

Impacts on the risk of an event, such as culling or death, are hazard
ratios, rate ratios, risk ratios, odds ratios or risk differences rather than
additive amounts. They are given with a `measure` (one per row; measures
can be mixed), crude or adjusted as above, and adjusted with
`event_model = TRUE` and the overall risk of the event over the period:

```{r}
cull <- cm_model(pop, cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(1.5, 2.0, 1.2),
                                 measure = c("HR", "HR", "RR"), outcome = "culling"))
res_cull <- deconflate(cull, event_model = TRUE, overall_risk = 0.25)
res_cull
```

The adjusted values are each disease's own hazard ratio, and the
contributions are each disease's share of the risk attributable to disease
(`$contributions`, the same columns as for additive impacts;
`$attributable$summary` has the overall, disease-free and attributable
risk). See `vignette("event-impacts")`.

## From adjusted impacts to gaps and values

`deconflate()` returns impacts and contributions in the units of the
impacts; it does not convert them into other quantities. Turning them into a
gap between the observed and the disease-free level of an outcome, or into a
value, needs to know what the impacts mean, and takes a few lines of base R.

When the impacts are percentage losses relative to the disease-free level
(as in `m`, with an observed mean of 10,000 units), the disease-free level is
`observed / (1 - aggregate / 100)`, the gap is the disease-free level minus
the observed level, and each disease's part of the gap is its share of the
aggregate:

```{r}
observed <- 10000
aggregate <- res$totals$adjusted_total            # in percent
disease_free <- observed / (1 - aggregate / 100)
gap <- disease_free - observed
ct <- res$contributions
by_disease <- data.frame(disease = ct$disease, gap = gap * ct$share)
by_disease
c(disease_free = disease_free, gap = gap)
```

A value per unit of outcome turns the gaps into values; any costs that are
not part of the adjustment are added separately:

```{r}
unit_value <- 0.30
by_disease$value <- by_disease$gap * unit_value
sum(by_disease$value)
```

`ct$share` is `NA` when the aggregate is zero; `disease_free * ct$contribution / 100`
gives the same gaps and stays defined. For an outcome that disease
increases, the disease-free level is `observed / (1 + aggregate / 100)` and the
gap is `observed - disease_free`. When the impacts are absolute effects (in
the outcome's own units, such as the days of the calving-interval model
`ci` above), no conversion is needed: each disease's contribution
(`ct$contribution`) is its part of the gap, and the aggregate is the gap. With
draws, the gap increases with the aggregate, so the same formula applied to
the interval bounds of the aggregate (`adjusted_total_lower` and
`adjusted_total_upper` in `$totals`) gives an interval for the total gap.

For event impacts, the attributable risk is already a proportion of
animals: times the herd size, it is the number of events (e.g. culls) that
disease adds over the period, and each disease's part is its contribution
(`$contributions$contribution`). A value per event (e.g. the replacement cost
less the salvage value) turns them into values:

```{r}
herd <- 100
ar <- res_cull$attributable
extra_culls <- herd * ar$summary$attributable
by_disease_cull <- data.frame(disease = res_cull$contributions$disease,
                              culls = herd * res_cull$contributions$contribution)
by_disease_cull$value <- by_disease_cull$culls * 1200   # per cull, illustrative
c(extra_culls = extra_culls, raw = herd * ar$summary$raw_attributable)
by_disease_cull
```

## Feasibility

Each pairwise table can be valid on its own while no population has all of
them. Fitting the distribution of disease combinations for the central
estimate checks that the rows can hold together:

```{r}
res$diagnostics$feasibility
```

Three diseases with probability 0.5, two strong positive associations and
one strong negative one cannot coexist:

```{r}
bad <- cm_model(
  cm_diseases(c("a", "b", "c"), c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5)),
  cm_impacts(c("a", "b", "c"), c(1, 2, 3)),
  associations = cm_associations(c("a", "a", "b"), c("b", "c", "c"), c(20, 20, 0.05))
)
check_feasibility(bad, method = "triples")
```

`check_feasibility()` screens every triple of diseases (a necessary
condition) and, with `method = "lp"`, runs an exact check of the pairwise
tables (it needs the `lpSolve` package).

## Conditions

Errors and warnings have classes, so that callers (and the draws and
sensitivity tools of the package) can handle them separately:

| Class | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `deconflate_infeasible` | inputs that admit no valid probabilities (e.g. the example above) |
| `deconflate_singular` | a singular or non-identifiable system |
| `deconflate_nonconvergence` | a numerical procedure did not converge |
| `deconflate_unsupported` | inputs or arguments that are not supported (or no longer used) |
| `deconflate_nonfinite` | non-finite results |
| `deconflate_input_problems` | `cm_read_inputs()` found errors in the input tables |

All errors also have class `deconflate_error`, and warnings
`deconflate_warning` (e.g. `deconflate_sign_change`).

```{r}
e <- tryCatch(deconflate(bad), deconflate_error = function(e) e)
class(e)
conditionMessage(e)
```

`deconflate()` also needs at least one association; without any, there is
nothing to de-conflate (the diseases would be treated as independent), and
it points to the tools that show how much associations could matter:

```{r}
no_assoc <- cm_model(pop$diseases, yield)
tryCatch(deconflate(no_assoc), deconflate_error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

## Checking the method with a simulated herd

`simulate_raw_impacts()` computes the raw impacts that single-disease studies
would report in a herd with known true impacts. Adjusting them should
recover the truth:

```{r}
m_sim <- cm_model(pop, simulate_raw_impacts(pop, c(d1 = 2, d2 = 4, d3 = 6)))
deconflate(m_sim)$adjusted[, c("disease", "raw", "adjusted")]
```

* `vignette("event-impacts")`: culling and other event impacts, and the risk
  attributable to disease.
* `vignette("interactions")`: the joint distribution, unknown associations,
  rows about combinations and subgroups, several rows per item, impact
  interactions and attribution.
* `vignette("uncertainty")`: draws and intervals, stability checks, rank
  shares and the sensitivity of the results to each input
  (`cm_sensitivity()`).
* `vignette("thresholds-and-scaling")`: threshold searches with
  `cm_threshold()` (at what input value does a ranking, a sign or the

  than about 20 diseases.
